en: August twenty three, twenty twenty three. India lands a spacecraft near the south pole of the Moon.
visual: REAL: ISRO Chandrayaan-3 landing-day footage: Vikram lander camera descent frames, then the ISTRAC control room erupting.
sound: Cold open: room tone of mission control, no music for 2 s

en: No country had ever landed there before.
visual: REAL: ISRO lander image of the lunar surface; slow push-in.

en: India builds its own nuclear submarines. It reached Mars on its very first try.
visual: REAL: INS Arihant at sea (Indian Navy / Commons); cut to ISRO Mars Orbiter Mission imagery (MOM image of Mars, ISRO).
onscreen: NUCLEAR SUBMARINE · INS ARIHANT · MARS ORBITER 2014

en: And yet... in hangars in Bengaluru and Nashik, brand new fighter jets are waiting.
visual: REAL: HAL Tejas Mk1A on the line at Nashik / Bengaluru (HAL, PIB, MoD photos), parallax push; ILLUSTRATION wireframe of the empty engine bay glowing amber.
sound: Hard audio stop on 'And yet', then hangar ambience

en: Painted. Radars fitted. Almost ready.
visual: Three macro cuts: grey paint, radome, cockpit canopy (HAL / Aero India photos, animated).

en: But not one of these new jets has joined the Air Force yet.
visual: Wide of the line of jets; counter in lower corner: DELIVERED TO IAF 0.

en: The biggest reason? They are waiting for an engine. An engine made in Lynn, Massachusetts, about thirteen thousand kilometres away.
visual: Kinetic globe (land only, no borders): an amber arc from Lynn, USA to Bengaluru; distance counter runs up.

en: So here is the question. India landed on the Moon. Why can it not build its own fighter jet engine?
visual: Split frame: Moon landing on the left, empty engine bay on the right; the title burns in between.
onscreen: INDIA LANDED ON THE MOON. WHY NOT A JET ENGINE?

en: Welcome to Be Practical with Kishore. Today, the story of one of the hardest machines on Earth to build. Single crystal metal, broken promises, and a forty year fight to join one of the world's most closed clubs.
visual: Logo sting, then title card over a macro of a glowing turbine blade: THE JET ENGINE PARADOX.
pacing: Logo sting on the channel name

en: To understand why one engine matters so much, look at the Indian Air Force.
visual: REAL: IAF fighters on a flight line, heat shimmer (IAF / Commons B-roll).

en: The Air Force is supposed to have forty two fighter squadrons. Today it has about twenty nine.
visual: Animated squadron gauge: 42 outlined slots, 29 fill in amber, 13 stay empty and pulse red.

en: Old jets like the MiG twenty one have retired. New jets are needed, fast.
visual: REAL: MiG-21 final flypast / retirement ceremony 2025 (credited excerpt or Commons).

en: So in twenty twenty one, the government ordered eighty three Tejas Mark One A jets from Hindustan Aeronautics, HAL. In twenty twenty five, it ordered ninety seven more.
visual: REAL: contract signing photo (PIB) with forensic magnifier on the figure; counter 83 → 180.

en: But HAL does not make the engine. Every one of these jets uses the F four zero four, made by GE Aerospace in America.
visual: REAL: GE F404 engine photos (GE press media / Commons), slow orbit parallax; ILLUSTRATION exploded view.
onscreen: ENGINE: GE F404-IN20 · MADE IN USA

en: The engines were due from twenty twenty three. The first one came only in March twenty twenty five.
visual: Kinetic timeline: 2023 promised marker slides right to MAR 2025 actual; gap fills red.

en: GE blamed problems in its supply chain. HAL put penalties on GE for the delay.
visual: Credited news headlines (Bloomberg / Business Standard) under magnifier.

en: By October twenty twenty six, GE had sent only fourteen of the ninety nine engines. HAL says close to thirty jets are built and waiting.
visual: Counter pair: ENGINES SENT 14 / 99 vs JETS BUILT 29; jets on the line pan.
cite: [GE AEROSPACE | NEW INDIAN EXPRESS | HAL CMD | OCT 2026]

en: Some testing work on radar and weapons is also still pending. But the engine has been the biggest hold up.
visual: REAL: Tejas Mk1A flying a test sortie (HAL/MoD footage).

en: And a delay is only the small problem. The real danger is control.
visual: Slow push on a single F404 under hard light; amber turns red.
sound: Music drops to a low pulse

en: India has been here before.
visual: Hard cut to black, then archive.

en: In May nineteen ninety eight, India tested nuclear weapons at Pokhran.
visual: REAL: Pokhran-II archive (Commons / DD News credited excerpt), Shakti site photo with parallax.

en: America answered with sanctions under a law called the Glenn Amendment.
visual: Credited archive: US press briefing on the sanctions, 1998 (Commons / archive.org); text of the law under magnifier.

en: Sales of the same GE F four zero four engines to India were stopped. American help on the Tejas flight controls also ended.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: Tejas prototype wireframe; the engine block and flight-control box fade out with a red STOPPED stamp.
onscreen: F404 SALES STOPPED · FLIGHT-CONTROL HELP ENDED

en: Indian engineers had to build the flight control system on their own. They did it.
visual: REAL: LCA Tejas early test flight archive (ADA/DRDO).

en: The lesson was simple. If you do not own the engine, you do not fully own your fighter jet.
visual: Slow push into a Tejas nozzle; heat haze.

en: Nine countries have nuclear bombs. About ten have put a satellite in space with their own rocket.
visual: Kinetic globe: 9 dots light up for nuclear-armed states, then about 10 for orbital launch states.

en: But only a handful can design and build a modern fighter engine on their own. The main ones are America, Russia, Britain and France. And, after decades of struggle, China.
visual: Kinetic globe, land only: five countries glow amber one by one with their makers (GE · Pratt & Whitney · NPO Saturn · Rolls-Royce · Safran · Chinese state makers); India outlined, empty.

en: India tried to join this club. And that started one of the hardest engineering stories in its history.
visual: Dissolve from the globe into a 1980s GTRE blueprint.

en: In nineteen eighty six, Indian engineers began planning their own fighter engine.
visual: Blueprint world: GTX-35VS Kaveri line drawing assembles stroke by stroke (ILLUSTRATION).

en: The job went to the Gas Turbine Research Establishment, GTRE, a DRDO lab in Bengaluru. The engine was named Kaveri.
visual: REAL: GTRE building / Kaveri engine at Aero India (Commons, credited).

en: Full development was approved in March nineteen eighty nine, with a budget of about three hundred and eighty two crore rupees.
visual: PROOF: PIB release (10 Dec 2012) under magnifier, highlight 'Rs.382.81 Crore'.

en: The plan was to finish by December nineteen ninety six.
visual: Same PIB page, magnifier slides to 'December 1996'.

en: The goal was huge. An engine that gives eighty one kilonewtons of push with the afterburner on.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: thrust arrow grows to an 81 kN target line.

en: And India was building a brand new jet, the Tejas, at the same time. Both almost from scratch. That doubled the risk.
visual: Split blueprint: Tejas airframe left, Kaveri engine right, both half-drawn and flickering.

en: When the Kaveri prototypes reached the test bench, the numbers did not add up.
visual: REAL: Kaveri on a ground test bed (DRDO/GTRE video or photo, credited).

en: It was meant to weigh eleven hundred kilos. It weighed twelve hundred and thirty five.
visual: Kinetic scale: needle swings past 1,100 to 1,235 kg; overweight band glows red.

en: It was meant to push eighty one kilonewtons. As reported, it reached only about seventy.
visual: Thrust bar fills to ~70 kN and stalls short of the 81 kN line.

en: And India had no facility to test a fighter engine in high altitude conditions.
visual: Map pulse: India, no altitude-test icon; the line jumps to Russia.

en: So Indian engineers had to take the Kaveri to Russia for those tests.
visual: Kinetic map, land only: Bengaluru to Moscow region (CIAM / Gromov, Zhukovsky).

en: The years went by. The Air Force could not wait for ever.
visual: Calendar years flip 1996 → 2008 over a dusty test cell.

en: In September two thousand eight, the Kaveri was officially separated from the Tejas programme. The Tejas would fly with the American engine.
visual: Credited headline (The Hindu, 27 Sep 2008) under magnifier; the Kaveri blueprint tears away from the Tejas blueprint.

en: But GTRE did not stop. In twenty ten, a Kaveri flew for the first time, fitted to a Russian Ilyushin transport plane used as a flying test bed.
visual: REAL: Il-76 flying test bed at Gromov Flight Research Institute (Commons, CC BY-SA), parallax.
onscreen: IL-76 FLYING TEST BED · GROMOV, RUSSIA · 2010

en: Twenty seven flights. Up to twelve kilometres high.
visual: Altitude counter runs to 12 km over the Il-76.

en: By twenty twelve, about two thousand crore rupees had been spent. The cost estimate had grown to over twenty eight hundred crore.
visual: PROOF: PIB page, magnifier on 'Rs.1996 Crore' and 'Rs.2839 Crore'; a counter climbs from 382 to 2,839.

en: So why did it fail? To answer that, we need to go inside the engine.
visual: Camera dives into a cutaway engine render (ILLUSTRATION).

en: First, a fair question. If ISRO can build rocket engines, why is a jet engine so much harder?
visual: Split: ISRO launch (real) left, fighter engine run (real) right.

en: A rocket engine fires for minutes, not hours. It carries its own oxygen. Then its job is done, and that stage falls away.
visual: REAL: LVM3 launch and stage separation (ISRO footage).

en: A fighter jet engine must breathe air. Humid sea air. Freezing mountain air. Desert dust.
visual: Three quick real cuts: coastal monsoon, Himalayan clouds, Rajasthan dust (stock, Indian locations).

en: It must go from idle to full power in seconds, again and again, during hard turns.
visual: REAL: fighter afterburner take-off at night (IAF / Commons).

en: And it must run for thousands of hours between overhauls.
visual: Hours counter spins to 4,000+ over an engine on a maintenance stand.

en: At the heart of it all is one small part. The high pressure turbine blade.
visual: Three.js: a single turbine blade rises out of darkness, amber rim light, slow 360° turn (ILLUSTRATION).

en: It sits right behind the combustion chamber, where burning fuel makes a storm of hot gas.
visual: Three.js cutaway: flame front in the combustor, gas flows through the turbine stage (ILLUSTRATION).

en: Now here is the shocking part.
visual: Hold on the blade, music cut.
sound: 1.5 s total music silence, then braam

en: Rolls-Royce says its blades work in gas up to two hundred degrees hotter than the melting point of the metal they are made of.
visual: Thermal-camera look (ironbow palette): gas temperature bar climbs past a MELTING POINT line on the blade.
onscreen: GAS: UP TO 200 °C ABOVE THE METAL'S MELTING POINT

en: The gas is hotter than the metal's melting point. And still the blade does not melt. How?
visual: Push into the glowing blade surface.

en: The first secret is in the metal itself.
visual: Zoom into the blade metal: crystals appear (ILLUSTRATION).

en: Normal metal is made of many tiny crystals. The borders between them are weak spots.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: multi-grain lattice, grain boundaries glow.

en: Under heat and huge force, the metal slowly stretches along those borders. Engineers call it creep.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: grains slide; blade lengthens slowly; label CREEP.

en: So the best blades are grown as one single crystal. No borders at all.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: perfect single-crystal lattice, atoms in one unbroken grid; then real photo of a single-crystal blade casting.

en: The metal is a nickel super alloy, with rare elements like rhenium mixed in.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: alloy recipe as glowing element tiles orbiting the blade (Ni, Co, Cr, Al, Ta, W, Re).

en: The second secret is air.
visual: Cut to blade cross-section.

en: Each blade is hollow, with tiny channels inside. Cooler air from the compressor is pushed through them.
visual: Three.js cutaway: serpentine cooling channels light up cyan as air flows through (ILLUSTRATION).

en: It comes out through rows of tiny holes, and covers the blade in a thin blanket of cooler air.
visual: Three.js: rows of film-cooling holes emit a thin cyan film that wraps the blade (ILLUSTRATION).

en: And on top, a ceramic coating acts like a heat shield.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: a ceramic layer (Ceramic White) seals the surface; temperature gradient shown through the wall.

en: Now add the spin. The disc holding these blades turns more than twelve thousand times every minute.
visual: Three.js: turbine disc spins up; rpm counter climbs past 12,000.

en: Rolls-Royce says the pull on each blade is like the weight of a London bus hanging from it.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: a red double-decker bus silhouette hangs from one blade in a slow-motion freeze.
onscreen: PULL ON ONE BLADE ≈ A LONDON BUS

en: Gas above the metal's melting point. A bus hanging from every blade. For thousands of hours.
visual: Fast triptych recap of the three images.

en: This is why so few countries can do it. You cannot just copy the drawing.
visual: Blueprint of a blade burns away to reveal a real casting.

en: The real knowledge is in how the metal is made, cast, drilled and tested. Countries learned it over decades of testing, and many failures.
visual: REAL: precision casting and laser-drilling B-roll (industrial stock), engine test cell run.

en: That knowledge is a closely guarded secret. For decades, no engine maker shared it with India.
visual: Close-up: a vault-like test cell door closes (stock).

en: But the Kaveri story did not end in two thousand eight.
visual: Return to the Kaveri blueprint; it re-ignites amber.

en: GTRE took out the afterburner and made a simpler version. The Dry Kaveri.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: the afterburner section slides off the Kaveri wireframe; label DRY KAVERI.

en: In tests in Russia, it gave about forty eight kilonewtons of push, a little more than its target.
visual: REAL: Kaveri derivative engine images (DRDO/PIB), thrust bar crosses 46 to 48.5 kN.

en: It is now chosen to power India's stealth combat drones, like the planned Ghatak.
visual: REAL: DRDO SWiFT flying-wing demonstrator footage (DRDO, 2022), labelled; then ILLUSTRATION of Ghatak.

en: Meanwhile, DRDO's metals lab in Hyderabad, DMRL, has learned to make single crystal turbine blades. First for a helicopter engine.
visual: REAL: DMRL single-crystal blade photos (PIB release, Apr 2021) under magnifier.

en: Those years of struggle were not wasted. They built the base India did not have in nineteen eighty six.
visual: Montage: Kaveri test cell, Il-76 FTB, DMRL blade; amber light grows.

en: But the next big fighter, the AMCA, needs much more.
visual: REAL: AMCA full-scale model at Aero India (Commons / PIB), parallax.

en: The first AMCA jets will use GE's F four one four engine.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: AMCA wireframe, twin F414s.

en: For later jets, India wants a new engine of about one hundred and twenty kilonewtons. And this time, it wants to own the design.
visual: ILLUSTRATION: a clean-sheet engine wireframe draws itself; label 120 kN CLASS.

en: In twenty twenty five, the government picked France's Safran to build it together with GTRE.
visual: REAL: Safran facility / M88 engine (Safran press media), map line Paris → Bengaluru.

en: India's condition is clear. The design and the rights must belong to India.
visual: Forensic highlight on a news report line about full IP ownership.

en: As of now, that deal is still waiting for final approval. And in August twenty twenty six, Rolls-Royce and Reliance also offered to build an engine in India.
visual: Credited headlines (Meta-Defense; Eurasia Review) under magnifier; a second line from Derby joins the map.

en: China walked this same road. Its J twenty stealth fighter used Russian engines at first. It took China decades, and many failures, to switch to engines of its own.
visual: REAL: J-20 photos (Commons); timeline AL-31F → WS-10C → WS-15.
onscreen: J-20: RUSSIAN AL-31F → CHINESE WS-10C → WS-15

en: So let us come back to our question.
visual: Moon landing and Tejas line side by side again.

en: Reaching the Moon needs rocket engines that work perfectly, but only for minutes at a time.
visual: Chandrayaan-3 descent replay, fast.

en: A fighter engine needs metal that lives in gas hotter than its own melting point, spinning, for thousands of hours.
visual: Blade glowing in the thermal look; rpm counter.

en: That is the jet engine paradox. The Moon was the easier problem.
visual: Title card burns in over the blade.

en: For forty years, India has been learning the hard way. Today, the Dry Kaveri is heading for certification, the blade makers in Hyderabad are learning, and a new engine is on the drawing board.
visual: Montage: Dry Kaveri, DMRL blade, AMCA model; dawn light over a test cell.

en: Will the Safran partnership finally give India a fighter engine of its own? Or will politics stall it again? Tell me what you think in the comments.
